manual.title: Keeping a Sourdough Starter Alive
manual.subtitle: Feeding schedules, rescue protocols, and who looks after it while you’re on holiday
manual.voice: A retired intensive-care nurse who has kept the same rye starter going for fourteen years and treats every jar as a patient in her care. She speaks in the gentle, unhurried bedside manner of someone who has calmed a great many frightened relatives: feeds are “rounds”, rise and smell are “vitals”, a neglected jar is “admitted” and a recovered one is “discharged”. The clinical framing is affectionate, never cold. Everything is measured — grams, never cups; degrees Celsius; hours between feeds — and every symptom is matched with a clear action. Her refrain is reassurance: a starter is far harder to kill than people fear. She is firm about one thing only: fuzzy mould or pink and orange streaks mean the patient is lost, and you start again.
